description: S2: Anna collects one microsecond before the deadline while the sweep expires her reservation

results.required, collection commits first: collect=200 collected expire=false | reservation=COLLECTED copy=ON_LOAN (held by none) openLoans=1 activeItems=1 notices=0
results.required, expiry commits first: collect=409 not active expire=true | reservation=EXPIRED copy=AVAILABLE (held by none) openLoans=0 activeItems=0 notices=1

notes: Both operations answered success in both orderings: Anna was told "collected" and "expired".
Collection first: the reservation says EXPIRED and the copy AVAILABLE, but Anna has an open loan of it. The next member can reserve a copy that is in Anna's bag.
Expiry first: the reservation says COLLECTED, so a test that checks only the status passes. Only the copy, the loans and the notices show the damage.

Why: plain reads, the decision in Java, and dirty checking's UPDATE reservation SET status=? WHERE id=? with no condition on the old status (see the SQL log). Collection also read the clock too early and ignored that lendOwned updated 0 copies.

description: S3: Anna's late "cancel" read the reservation; she collects at the desk; the cancel goes on

results.required: cancel=409 not active collect=200 collected | reservation=COLLECTED copy=ON_LOAN (held by none) openLoans=1 activeItems=1 notices=0

notes: The cancel took a real lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in the SQL log) and still decided on ACTIVE: the lock query returned the Reservation object already in the persistence context, with the fields it had before waiting.
Anna has the book on loan, and the system put it back on the shelf.

description: S4: Anna's reservation expired, Bruno reserved the copy, then the sweep reached Anna's
notes: No concurrency at all. Lazy expiry let Bruno take the copy before any sweep; the naive sweep then made it AVAILABLE without checking who held it.
Bruno's reservation is ACTIVE but holds nothing, so Clara got the same copy: two live promises for one copy.

description: S5: the sweep locks reservation, copies, member; Anna's new reservation locks member, copies
notes: Each holds the lock the other one waits for. PostgreSQL detects the cycle after deadlock_timeout (1 s) and aborts one of them with SQL state 40P01.
Nobody hangs, but a request with nothing wrong in it fails. If it is Anna's, she gets an error for a perfectly valid reservation.

description: S6: two application instances sweep the same 100 expired reservations
notes: The stored rows look right: EXPIRED twice is still EXPIRED, AVAILABLE twice is still AVAILABLE. Only the side effects show the bug: every member got two notices.
fixedDelay keeps one scheduler from overlapping with itself; two instances have two schedulers. Only the database can arbitrate between them.

description: S6b: three expired reservations; the second fails right after its notice was sent
notes: The notice is sent inside the transaction. The transaction rolled back, the notice did not: a member was told that a reservation expired, and it is still ACTIVE.
Something left the system that the database does not confirm: the library's version of "charged, but no ticket".

description: S7: a backlog of 1000 expired reservations, swept in one transaction
notes: Every expire() joined the sweep's transaction: all the reservations, copies and members stayed in one persistence context, and each auto-flush dirty-checked all of them.
A released copy stays locked until the final commit: Bruno waited for the whole sweep.
One failure rolled back every expiry, while the notices already sent stayed sent.

description: S8: the return machine retries Anna's return; Bruno reserves the copy between the two
notes: Both returns read the copy as ON_LOAN. The second one's UPDATE writes every column of its stale Copy (status, reservation_id, reserved_until), not only the ones that changed: Bruno's reservation lost the copy.
Bruno's reservation is ACTIVE and holds nothing, so Clara got the copy too.
